name: Cardiology
description: ECGs, murmurs, eponyms, drugs, scores and landmark trials, from wards to fellowship.
info: ECG strips: Wikimedia Commons under free licences, credited per image. Not medical advice.
question: {prompt}

cards.prompt: ECG from an 89-year-old with palpitations: name the rhythm.
cards.fact: In nonvalvular AF, about 90% of left atrial thrombi form in the left atrial appendage.

image.alt: 12-lead ECG with narrow QRS complexes at uneven intervals and a wavy baseline

cards.prompt: ECG with arrows on the baseline waves: name the rhythm.
cards.fact: Typical flutter circles the tricuspid annulus; ablating the cavotricuspid isthmus cures most cases.

image.alt: 12-lead ECG with regular, repeating baseline waves between narrow QRS complexes, marked by arrows

cards.prompt: Lead II monitor strip from a 40-year-old at 179 bpm: name the rhythm.
cards.fact: AVNRT is the most common regular paroxysmal SVT; vagal maneuvers or adenosine block the AV node to stop it.

image.alt: Single-lead monitor strip of a fast, regular, narrow-complex rhythm

cards.prompt: 12-lead ECG of a regular wide-complex tachycardia: name the rhythm.
cards.fact: Treat a wide-complex tachycardia as VT until proven otherwise, especially with structural heart disease.

image.alt: 12-lead ECG of a fast, regular rhythm with broad, uniform QRS complexes
image.credit: Ksheka at English Wikipedia via Wikimedia Commons

cards.prompt: 12-lead ECG from a pulseless patient: name the rhythm.
cards.fact: VF and pulseless VT are the shockable arrest rhythms; asystole and PEA are not.

image.alt: 12-lead ECG of chaotic, irregular undulations with no organized complexes

cards.prompt: Telemetry strip; the blue line traces the twisting QRS axis. Name the rhythm.
cards.fact: IV magnesium is first-line for torsades, even when the serum magnesium is normal.

image.alt: Telemetry strip of a fast, broad-complex rhythm whose peaks wax and wane, traced by a blue line

cards.prompt: Monitor strip from a hypotensive patient: P waves and QRS complexes each march on at their own rate. Name the rhythm.
cards.fact: A narrow escape rhythm suggests a junctional (nodal) level block; a wide escape suggests an infranodal one.

image.alt: Two-lead monitor strip with regular P waves and slower, regular QRS complexes
image.credit: MoodyGroove at English Wikipedia via Wikimedia Commons

cards.prompt: Schematic rhythm strip: one P wave fails to conduct, and the PR is shortest just after the pause. Name the AV block.
cards.fact: Usually AV nodal and often benign, e.g. in athletes during sleep; the PR increments shrink as the cycle goes on.

image.alt: Drawn rhythm strip of P waves and QRS complexes with one pause

cards.prompt: 12-lead ECG with a short PR and a slurred QRS upstroke: name the pattern.
cards.fact: In pre-excited AF, avoid AV nodal blockers: they can speed conduction down the pathway and trigger VF.

image.alt: 12-lead ECG in sinus rhythm with slightly broad QRS complexes
image.credit: Ksheka at English Wikipedia via Wikimedia Commons

cards.prompt: Sudden dropped QRS complexes with a constant PR in the conducted beats: which AV block?
cards.fact: Mobitz II is usually infranodal and can progress suddenly to complete heart block; it warrants a pacemaker.

cards.prompt: ECG with an rsR′ in V1 and a broad, slurred S wave in I and V6: name the conduction pattern.
cards.fact: Unlike LBBB, RBBB leaves the first part of the QRS intact, so Q waves of infarction stay readable.

image.alt: 12-lead ECG in sinus rhythm with broad, notched QRS complexes in the right chest leads

cards.prompt: ECG in a young adult with sharp chest pain eased by sitting forward: diagnosis?
cards.fact: Look for diffuse concave ST elevation, PR depression, and ST depression with PR elevation in aVR.

image.alt: 12-lead ECG in sinus rhythm with ST segments raised across many leads
image.credit: James Heilman, MD via Wikimedia Commons

cards.prompt: Pain-free ECG hours after an episode of chest pain, with deep symmetric T inversion in V2–V6: name the syndrome.
cards.fact: Wellens T waves signal critical proximal LAD stenosis; stress testing is dangerous, and angiography is needed.

image.alt: 12-lead ECG in sinus rhythm with deep, symmetric T-wave inversion in the chest leads
image.credit: James Heilman, MD via Wikimedia Commons

cards.prompt: Tachycardia with low voltage and QRS amplitude alternating beat to beat: what is the likely cause?
cards.fact: The heart swings back and forth within a large effusion, changing its electrical axis with every beat.

image.alt: 12-lead ECG of a fast, low-voltage rhythm with QRS heights varying from beat to beat
image.credit: James Heilman, MD via Wikimedia Commons

cards.prompt: ECG from a patient with advanced kidney disease, with tall, narrow, peaked T waves: which electrolyte disturbance?
cards.fact: IV calcium stabilizes the myocardium within minutes but does not lower potassium; insulin and dialysis do.

image.alt: 12-lead ECG with tall, narrow, pointed T waves in the chest leads
image.credit: Dr. Michael-Joseph F. Agbayani and Dr. Eddieson Gonzales via Wikimedia Commons

cards.prompt: ECG of a patient after unexplained syncope: coved ST elevation and T inversion in V1–V2. Name the pattern.
cards.fact: Fever and sodium-channel blockers can unmask a type 1 pattern; placing V1–V2 one or two spaces higher helps too.

image.alt: 12-lead ECG with downsloping ST elevation and inverted T waves in V1 and V2
image.credit: CardioNetworks ECGpedia (courtesy of P.G. Postema, MD) via Wikimedia Commons

cards.prompt: ECG with very deep S waves in V2–V3, tall R waves in V5, and lateral ST-T "strain": name the finding.
cards.fact: Voltage criteria such as Sokolow–Lyon are specific but insensitive for LVH; echo or MRI is far better.

image.alt: 12-lead ECG with very large QRS voltages and lateral T-wave inversion
image.credit: James Heilman, MD via Wikimedia Commons

cards.prompt: ECG in acute chest pain with ST elevation across V2–V5: which artery is the likely culprit?
cards.fact: Occlusion proximal to the first diagonal often adds ST elevation in I and aVL, with reciprocal inferior depression.

image.alt: 12-lead ECG with large, domed ST elevation in the chest leads

cards.prompt: ECG in acute chest pain (with right-sided and posterior leads): ST elevation in II, III and aVF localizes to which wall?
cards.fact: Inferior MI is usually an RCA occlusion; ST elevation in III greater than II favors the RCA over the circumflex.

image.alt: 15-lead ECG with marked ST elevation in several limb leads and depression in others
image.credit: James Heilman, MD via Wikimedia Commons

cards.prompt: Which right-sided precordial lead is most useful for detecting right ventricular infarction?
cards.fact: RV infarction is preload-dependent: nitrates can crash the pressure, and fluids are the first move for hypotension.

cards.prompt: ST depression in V1–V3 with tall R waves, and ST elevation in V7–V9, indicates which infarct?
cards.fact: Posterior leads V7–V9 sit on the left back; the anterior ST depression is the posterior injury seen in mirror image.

cards.prompt: Upsloping ST depression with tall, symmetric precordial T waves (de Winter pattern) signals occlusion of which artery?
cards.fact: De Winter T waves are a STEMI equivalent: they often lack classic ST elevation yet warrant emergent reperfusion.

cards.prompt: The Sgarbossa criteria help diagnose acute MI in the presence of which conduction pattern?
cards.fact: Smith-modified Sgarbossa swaps the 5 mm discordance rule for a proportional ST/S ratio of −0.25 or less.

cards.prompt: An S wave in I, Q wave in III and inverted T in III (S1Q3T3) is classically linked to which diagnosis?
cards.fact: S1Q3T3 is specific but insensitive; sinus tachycardia is the most common ECG finding in PE.

cards.prompt: Hypocalcemia lengthens the ST segment and so prolongs which ECG interval?
cards.fact: Calcium works the other way too: hypercalcemia shortens the QT.

cards.prompt: Which drug causes "scooped," sagging ST depression, sometimes likened to Salvador Dalí's mustache?
cards.fact: Digoxin effect is not toxicity; toxicity classically brings bidirectional VT or atrial tachycardia with block.

cards.prompt: Epsilon waves, small notches just after the QRS in V1–V3, are a hallmark of which cardiomyopathy?
cards.fact: ARVC is mostly a disease of desmosomal genes, such as PKP2; endurance exercise accelerates it.

cards.prompt: Which congenital long QT type typically causes events while swimming or exercising?
cards.fact: LQT1 (KCNQ1) events come with exercise, LQT2 (KCNH2) with sudden noises, LQT3 (SCN5A) during sleep or rest.

cards.prompt: Painless, flat red macules on the palm in a febrile patient with a new murmur are called what?
cards.fact: Osler nodes are painful and immune-mediated; Janeway lesions are painless septic microemboli.

image.alt: Close-up of a palm dotted with small, flat, reddish macules

cards.prompt: Hypotension, distended neck veins and muffled heart sounds (Beck's triad) point to what?
cards.fact: Claude Beck, a Cleveland surgeon, described his compression triads in 1935; few tamponade patients show all three.

cards.prompt: An inspiratory fall in systolic blood pressure of more than 10 mmHg is called what?
cards.fact: Kussmaul called it "paradoxical" because the radial pulse vanished while the heartbeat was still heard.

cards.prompt: A paradoxical rise in jugular venous pressure on inspiration is whose sign?
cards.fact: Kussmaul's sign is classic for constrictive pericarditis and is typically absent in tamponade.

cards.prompt: A crescendo–decrescendo systolic murmur at the right upper sternal border radiating to the carotids suggests what?
cards.fact: Signs of severe AS: a late-peaking murmur, a soft or absent A2, and a slow-rising carotid pulse (parvus et tardus).

cards.prompt: A holosystolic, blowing apical murmur radiating to the axilla suggests what?
cards.fact: Acute severe MR, as with papillary muscle rupture, can have a soft or even absent murmur.

cards.prompt: The murmur of obstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy gets louder with which maneuver?
cards.fact: Less preload means a smaller LV cavity and more outflow obstruction; squatting and handgrip soften the murmur.

cards.prompt: A late-diastolic sound just before S1, from atrial contraction into a stiff ventricle, is called what?
cards.fact: An S4 needs an atrial kick, so you cannot hear one in atrial fibrillation.

cards.prompt: Wide, fixed splitting of S2 is the classic auscultatory sign of which lesion?
cards.fact: Paradoxical (reversed) splitting of S2 points instead to LBBB or severe aortic stenosis.

cards.prompt: A mid-diastolic apical rumble heard in severe aortic regurgitation is which eponymous murmur?
cards.fact: The regurgitant jet buffets the anterior mitral leaflet, producing a functional mitral stenosis.

cards.prompt: The early diastolic murmur of pulmonary regurgitation due to pulmonary hypertension is which eponymous murmur?
cards.fact: Like most right-sided murmurs it is heard at the left upper sternal border and grows louder with inspiration.

cards.prompt: Visible capillary pulsations in the nail bed in aortic regurgitation are whose sign?
cards.fact: The head bob of AR is de Musset's sign, named after the French poet Alfred de Musset.

cards.prompt: A tricuspid regurgitation murmur that gets louder with inspiration is whose sign?
cards.fact: Inspiration increases venous return to the right heart, so right-sided murmurs usually intensify.

cards.prompt: A shorter interval between A2 and the opening snap means more severe disease of which valve?
cards.fact: Higher left atrial pressure pops the mitral valve open sooner; rheumatic disease is the main cause worldwide.

cards.prompt: Which drug is the specific reversal agent for dabigatran?
cards.fact: Idarucizumab is a humanized monoclonal antibody fragment that binds dabigatran far more tightly than thrombin does.

cards.prompt: Which recombinant, catalytically inactive "decoy" factor Xa reverses apixaban and rivaroxaban?
cards.fact: It also binds tissue factor pathway inhibitor; thrombotic events are a known risk after reversal.

cards.prompt: Which positively charged protein reverses unfractionated heparin?
cards.fact: Protamine only partly reverses low-molecular-weight heparin and does not reverse fondaparinux.

cards.prompt: Life-threatening digoxin toxicity is treated with which antidote?
cards.fact: Hyperkalemia in acute digoxin poisoning reflects Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase blockade and predicts mortality.

cards.prompt: Which antiarrhythmic can cause pulmonary fibrosis, thyroid dysfunction and blue-gray skin?
cards.fact: Amiodarone is roughly 37% iodine by weight and has a half-life measured in weeks.

cards.prompt: After CAST, which Vaughan Williams class (e.g. flecainide) is avoided in patients with prior MI?
cards.fact: CAST (1989) was stopped early: suppressing post-MI ectopy with encainide or flecainide increased mortality.

cards.prompt: Sacubitril, paired with valsartan as an ARNI, inhibits which enzyme?
cards.fact: Never combine an ARNI with an ACE inhibitor: a 36-hour washout is needed because of angioedema risk.

cards.prompt: SGLT2 inhibitors such as dapagliflozin act on which nephron segment?
cards.fact: Their heart failure benefit is seen with or without diabetes; euglycemic ketoacidosis is a rare but key risk.

cards.prompt: Which mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist commonly causes gynecomastia through anti-androgen effects?
cards.fact: Eplerenone is far more receptor-selective, so gynecomastia is rare; both can raise potassium.

cards.prompt: Ivabradine slows the sinus node by blocking which current?
cards.fact: It only works in sinus rhythm; luminous visual phenomena (phosphenes) are a characteristic side effect.

cards.prompt: Nitrates are contraindicated with which drug class because of profound hypotension?
cards.fact: Both raise cyclic GMP in vascular smooth muscle, so their vasodilating effects multiply.

cards.prompt: Warfarin works by inhibiting which enzyme?
cards.fact: Protein C falls fastest, so early warfarin can be prothrombotic, the mechanism of warfarin skin necrosis.

cards.prompt: Loss-of-function alleles of which CYP gene blunt clopidogrel's antiplatelet effect?
cards.fact: Clopidogrel is a prodrug; the FDA boxed warning concerns CYP2C19 poor metabolizers.

cards.prompt: Which oral, reversibly binding P2Y12 inhibitor is known for causing dyspnea?
cards.fact: The dyspnea is thought to be adenosine-mediated; ticagrelor is active itself and needs no metabolic activation.

cards.prompt: Prasugrel is contraindicated in patients with a history of what?
cards.fact: In TRITON-TIMI 38, prior stroke/TIA patients had net harm, with more intracranial bleeding.

cards.prompt: Which antiarrhythmic's effect is potentiated by dipyridamole and blunted by caffeine?
cards.fact: Heart transplant recipients have denervated, supersensitive hearts and respond exaggeratedly to adenosine.

cards.prompt: Statins inhibit which enzyme, the rate-limiting step of cholesterol synthesis?
cards.fact: Bempedoic acid blocks ATP citrate lyase upstream and is activated only in the liver, sparing muscle.

cards.prompt: Evolocumab and alirocumab are monoclonal antibodies against which protein?
cards.fact: Inclisiran also targets PCSK9, but as an siRNA that silences its production in the liver.

cards.prompt: Mavacamten, used for obstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, inhibits what?
cards.fact: By reducing actin–myosin cross-bridges it lowers outflow gradients; LVEF must be monitored on therapy.

cards.prompt: In CHA₂DS₂-VASc, what does the 2-point "A₂" stand for?
cards.fact: The other 2-pointer is S₂: prior stroke, TIA or thromboembolism. Age 65–74 scores 1 point.

cards.prompt: What is the maximum possible CHA₂DS₂-VASc score?
cards.fact: The 2024 ESC AF guideline dropped the sex category, using CHA₂DS₂-VA (maximum 8).

cards.prompt: In the HAS-BLED bleeding score, what does the "L" stand for?
cards.fact: A high HAS-BLED flags modifiable bleeding risks to fix; by itself it is not a reason to withhold anticoagulation.

cards.prompt: Heart failure with symptoms on less-than-ordinary activity but comfortable at rest is which NYHA class?
cards.fact: NYHA class can go up and down; ACC/AHA stages A–D describe progression and never move backward.

cards.prompt: Which ACC/AHA heart failure stage describes patients at risk (e.g. hypertension) with no structural heart disease?
cards.fact: Since 2022, stage B is "pre-heart failure": structural disease or raised biomarkers without symptoms.

cards.prompt: In acute MI, cardiogenic shock corresponds to which Killip class?
cards.fact: Killip and Kimball proposed the scheme in 1967 from coronary care unit patients; class III is pulmonary edema.

cards.prompt: Normal, brisk antegrade coronary flow on angiography is which TIMI flow grade?
cards.fact: TIMI 0 is no flow past the occlusion; TIMI 2 fills the whole vessel, but sluggishly.

cards.prompt: The Duke criteria are used to diagnose what?
cards.fact: Rheumatic fever has its own scheme, the Jones criteria; Duke was updated as Duke-ISCVID in 2023.

cards.prompt: In the HEART score for chest pain, what does the final "T" stand for?
cards.fact: HEART = History, ECG, Age, Risk factors, Troponin; a score of 0–3 marks low risk.

cards.prompt: Coronary dominance is defined by which coronary artery gives rise to which branch?
cards.fact: About 80% of people are right dominant; in left-dominant hearts the circumflex gives off the PDA.

cards.prompt: In a right-dominant heart, the AV nodal artery usually arises from which vessel?
cards.fact: This is why inferior MI often brings AV block, usually at the node and often transient.

cards.prompt: Which coronary artery is nicknamed the "widowmaker" when occluded proximally?
cards.fact: The LAD supplies the anterior wall, apex and most of the septum, a large share of the LV myocardium.

cards.prompt: The compact AV node lies at the apex of which anatomical triangle?
cards.fact: Its borders: the tendon of Todaro, the septal tricuspid leaflet and the coronary sinus ostium.

cards.prompt: Stroke volume rises as end-diastolic volume increases: which law?
cards.fact: More stretch improves actin–myosin overlap and calcium sensitivity, so the next beat is stronger.

cards.prompt: On a left ventricular pressure–volume loop, what does the loop's width represent?
cards.fact: The loop's area is stroke work; the slope of the end-systolic pressure–volume relation indexes contractility.

cards.prompt: Cardiac output = oxygen consumption ÷ arteriovenous O₂ content difference. Whose principle?
cards.fact: Thermodilution, the other cath-lab method, is unreliable with severe tricuspid regurgitation.

cards.prompt: In the simplified Bernoulli equation, the pressure gradient equals 4 times what?
cards.fact: A peak aortic jet of 4 m/s means a peak gradient of 64 mmHg, the threshold for severe AS.

cards.prompt: Which echo calculation estimates aortic valve area from LVOT and aortic jet velocities?
cards.fact: LVOT diameter is squared in the formula, so a small measurement error makes a big difference in valve area.

cards.prompt: Left ventricular myocardium is perfused mainly during which part of the cardiac cycle?
cards.fact: Tachycardia shortens diastole more than systole, which is one reason slowing the heart relieves angina.

cards.prompt: Transient apical ballooning of the LV after severe emotional stress, with no culprit coronary lesion, is called what?
cards.fact: Named after a Japanese octopus trap; most patients are postmenopausal women.

cards.prompt: Discordant LV and RV systolic pressures with respiration on catheterization favor which diagnosis?
cards.fact: A rigid pericardium makes the ventricles compete for space; restrictive cardiomyopathy shows concordant pressures.

cards.prompt: A left-to-right shunt that reverses because of severe pulmonary vascular disease is called what?
cards.fact: With a PDA, Eisenmenger causes differential cyanosis: blue, clubbed toes but pink fingers.

cards.prompt: VSD, overriding aorta, RV outflow obstruction and RV hypertrophy make up which lesion?
cards.fact: Children with "tet spells" squat: raising systemic resistance pushes blood back through the lungs.

cards.prompt: Apical displacement of the septal tricuspid leaflet with an "atrialized" right ventricle is which anomaly?
cards.fact: Accessory pathways (WPW) are common in Ebstein anomaly, often on the right side.

cards.prompt: An atrial septal defect combined with mitral stenosis is which eponymous syndrome?
cards.fact: Holt–Oram is different: an ASD with upper-limb (thumb or radial) defects, caused by TBX5 mutations.

cards.prompt: Rib notching on chest X-ray and radio-femoral pulse delay suggest which diagnosis?
cards.fact: Coarctation often comes with a bicuspid aortic valve, and is a classic association of Turner syndrome.

cards.prompt: Pericarditis with fever arising weeks after a myocardial infarction is which syndrome?
cards.fact: Thought to be immune-mediated, Dressler syndrome has become rare in the era of early reperfusion.

cards.prompt: Endocarditis due to Streptococcus gallolyticus (formerly S. bovis) should prompt which test?
cards.fact: S. gallolyticus bacteremia is strongly associated with colorectal adenomas and cancer.

cards.prompt: DOACs are contraindicated for anticoagulation in patients with which type of heart valve?
cards.fact: RE-ALIGN (2013) was stopped early: dabigatran caused more clots and more bleeding than warfarin.

cards.prompt: Which nuclear scan can diagnose transthyretin cardiac amyloidosis without biopsy, once AL is excluded?
cards.fact: Light-chain (AL) amyloid must be ruled out first with serum and urine tests, since it can also take up tracer.

cards.prompt: Which 1988 trial showed that aspirin and streptokinase each cut mortality after MI, with additive benefit?
cards.fact: ISIS-2 enrolled over 17,000 patients; aspirin alone cut 5-week vascular mortality by about a quarter.

cards.prompt: RALES (1999) showed a mortality benefit in severe HFrEF from adding which drug?
cards.fact: RALES was stopped early for a 30% relative reduction in death; eplerenone was later proven in EMPHASIS-HF.

cards.prompt: PARADIGM-HF compared sacubitril–valsartan with which drug in HFrEF?
cards.fact: Stopped early for benefit in 2014: fewer cardiovascular deaths and heart failure hospitalizations.

cards.prompt: Which 2019 trial first showed an SGLT2 inhibitor improves outcomes in HFrEF, with or without diabetes?
cards.fact: EMPEROR-Reduced (2020) confirmed the benefit with empagliflozin.

cards.prompt: Which 2021 trial was the first large HFpEF trial to meet its primary endpoint, using empagliflozin?
cards.fact: TOPCAT (spironolactone), PARAGON-HF (sacubitril–valsartan) and I-PRESERVE (irbesartan) all missed theirs.

cards.prompt: Which 2007 trial found that adding PCI to optimal medical therapy in stable CAD did not reduce death or MI?
cards.fact: ISCHEMIA (2020) extended this to moderate–severe ischemia: no fewer major events with routine invasive care.

cards.prompt: Which 2018 trial found catheter ablation of AF reduced death or HF hospitalization in HFrEF?
cards.fact: CABANA (2019), in a broader AF population, did not show a significant benefit on its intention-to-treat endpoint.

cards.prompt: Which 2020 trial showed early rhythm control, within a year of AF diagnosis, reduced cardiovascular outcomes?
cards.fact: AFFIRM (2002) had found no survival advantage for rhythm over rate control, using older drugs.

cards.prompt: Which 2018 trial showed transcatheter edge-to-edge mitral repair reduced HF hospitalization and death in secondary MR?
cards.fact: MITRA-FR, published the same year, was neutral; COAPT enrolled more severe MR with less dilated ventricles.

cards.prompt: Which trial showed adding ezetimibe to simvastatin after ACS modestly reduced cardiovascular events?
cards.fact: Published in 2015, it supported "lower is better" for LDL even when achieved with a non-statin drug.

cards.prompt: PARTNER 3 and Evolut Low Risk (2019) tested TAVR against surgery in which surgical-risk group?
cards.fact: TAVR was first proven in inoperable patients: PARTNER cohort B (2010) showed lower mortality vs. standard therapy.
